rule: Boundaries `treebank shape` may ignore, as `"<tscKind> <- <our_kind>"` pairs. Each is a place our tree groups the code DIFFERENTLY from tsc on purpose, not a place we disagree about the code. Pairs rather than bare tsc kinds: ignoring `PropertySignature` outright would also silence a real PropertySignature disagreement somewhere else, which is how a check like this quietly stops working. Every entry below was read and confirmed by hand; nothing goes in here to make a number go down.

ignore.why: tsc splits a variable statement into modifiers + a declaration LIST; we have one `variable_declaration` covering modifiers, declarators and the terminator. `declare const x: T;` gives tsc a list spanning `const x: T` with no node of ours at that start, because ours begins at `declare`.
Same split inside `for (const k in o)`. tsc has a declaration list around `const k`; our `for_in_statement` names `left` directly.
tsc's ImportClause includes the `type` keyword of `import type { A }`; our `import_clause` starts after it, with `type` as a sibling token.

We have no node for an interface's `extends` list — the types hang directly off `interface_definition`. A real `heritage_clause` node would be an improvement, not a correction; recorded here so the difference is a decision rather than a surprise.
tsc gives `class C extends A implements B` TWO heritage clauses; our single `class_heritage` spans both. Same call as above.
The `k: string` of `[k: string]: V` is a Parameter to tsc; we expose it as `name` and `index_type` fields of `index_signature` with no wrapping node.
The `K in keyof T` of a mapped type is a TypeParameter to tsc; we model the `in` form inside `mapped_type` rather than as a type parameter.
`export * as ns from 'm'` — tsc wraps `* as ns`; we keep the parts as siblings of `export_statement`.

tsc decomposes a template literal into Head / Span / Middle / Tail, each of which straddles a `}...${` boundary. We model it as alternating `string_content` and `template_substitution`, so no node of ours spans a substitution's close brace plus the following text. A different decomposition of the same string, not a different reading of it. Applies to the four TemplateSpan/Head/Middle/LastTemplateToken entries here and their `template_literal_type` twins.
See `TemplateSpan <- template_string`.
See `TemplateSpan <- template_string`.

See `TemplateSpan <- template_string`; same decomposition, type position.

tsc wraps a catch parameter in a VariableDeclaration; we expose it as `parameter` and `type` fields of `catch_clause` with no wrapping node. Same call as `Parameter <- index_signature`.

tsc wraps an element's attributes in a JsxAttributes container; ours are direct children of the element. No information is lost -- they are already unambiguously that element's attributes -- so this is the same call as `arguments` or `class_heritage`.
See `JsxAttributes <- jsx_self_closing_element`.

tsc models the comma operator as a left-associative BinaryExpression, so `a, b, c` nests; we model it as one flat `sequence_expression`. Different shape for the same operator, and ours is the one the vocabulary wants -- see the `sequence_expression` note in roles.json.

baseline_note: Down from 3,229. What remains is the three entries in known_limits — 6 files, each a GLR tie where the two readings hold identical node multisets, so there is nothing for dynamic precedence to weigh. Raising this number is a decision that belongs in a commit message.

known_limits.why: `infer R extends PropertyKey[][]` binds one `[]` into the constraint and leaves the other outside. The single-`[]` case was fixed by weighting `_no_conditional_type`'s growable alternatives, but at two levels the readings are exactly symmetric: whichever way it nests, precisely one `array_type` is reached through `_no_conditional_type`, so any bonus cancels. The real fix is to forbid a bare `infer_type` as the base of `array_type` -- `(infer R extends P)[]` needs parentheses in TypeScript anyway -- which costs a duplicated type tier. Not worth it for 4 files.

`await f<T>(x)` binds as `(await f)<T>(x)`. `[binary_expression, await_expression, call_expression]` is a declared GLR conflict and the two readings hold IDENTICAL node multisets -- one await, one call, one type_arguments each -- so dynamic precedence has nothing to weigh. Would need the ambiguity removed structurally.
